Crush is the live price-supportive leg (board crush margin 2.43 USD/bu on 23 September 2026, 89th percentile [N115][N117]); on the three-month horizon the record carries only two comparable past cases with a price reading over the band, too thin for a middle figure — history, not a forecast.
raw_draft.postverify_mechanism:
## Mechanism
**The tight-buffer leg.** US stocks-to-use is declared to move price in the opposite direction at high confidence: a thinner buffer means each incremental demand ton must be rationed by price rather than by inventory. At the 23rd percentile of its own record [N96], the response to a shock is convex on the upside and a good crop is absorbed rather than dumped.

**The crush demand-pull leg.** Crude oil against its own five-year record reads 0.51 z, August 2026 [N119]; the model expects it to lift the board crush margin, and the readings agree. Crush margin at 2.43 USD/bu [N115] pulls bean demand forward; the model expects that to pull stocks-to-use down, and the readings agree again. The last link into flat price — the calendar spread — has no series served here, so the chain quantifies to the balance sheet and stops before the board. Of the past times crude sat this far out, the crush margin moved the model's way in five cases and against it in three.

**The pressuring leg.** The warm Pacific phase is declared opposite-sign on beans at medium confidence, lag one to two quarters; its effect window runs to about January 2027, so the three-month horizon sits inside it. US harvested area at 34.76 M ha, 91st percentile [N109][N111], and Argentine production at 50 MMT [N106] both lean the same way. Against them, US drought and flash-drought readings are on the wet side (-0.69 z, August 2026 [N67]), so there is no weather squeeze in the current record — the South American weather-squeeze pattern shows one of the five conditions it names and asks for three.

**Which dominates.** The crush pattern's count is at its own threshold (two of the conditions it names, counted once after the crush aliases collapse); the glut and trade-war patterns are both short of theirs, and each has a reading in the tail opposite the one it names. So the net tilt is modestly price-supportive on a thin buffer, with the warm-phase channel the credible offset if South American supply builds.

**Crowding.** Managed money holds 241,501 contracts, the 99th percentile of its own record, easing over the last week [N52][N54]. That is context, not a cause the model declares — but it is why a reversal, if the warm-phase leg wins, would be abrupt rather than gradual.

## The record
- November 2026 soybeans settled 1317.5 US cents/bushel on 24 September 2026 [N138], up 176 over sixty-three sessions [N142] and down 2.25 over five [N140].
- USDA projects 2026/27 US ending stocks at 310 Million Bushels on production of 4,535 Million Bushels, known 11 September 2026 [N2][N3]; US crop 58 pct good-to-excellent and 12 pct harvested, known 22 September 2026 [N11][N10].

Our price history for MATIF rapeseed and CME palm oil does not reach that window.

## Mechanism

Two legs, opposite signs, and the tiebreaker is confidence.

- **Supply**: smaller production with unchanged offtake draws the carryout down. Lower ending stocks against a fixed domestic use shrink the cushion, and in the driver model a falling stocks-to-use ratio is a high-confidence support to price.
- **Weather**: the warm Pacific phase is the largest reading on this market and the driver model gives it the opposite sign on cotton at medium confidence, one to three quarters — wetter US Southwest, better South Asian monsoon, easier yields, a looser world sheet. A USDA attaché report of 3 April 2026 frames the other tail: if warm-phase conditions emerge during 2026 they could weaken the Indian monsoon and raise drought and heat risk [E36] — an expectation as of that report, not a realised outcome.
- **Demand and trade**: Chinese mill consumption is projected 9.14 MMT [N67], the 90.3th percentile of its own record [N69], rising five straight years — price-supportive at medium confidence. Against it, US exports read 2.68 MMT [N80] at the 76th percentile [N82]; the model treats the trade-policy and export-pace names as one reading on this series, not two. A 10 percent tariff on US-origin cotton was reported 22 April 2026 to have rendered it uncompetitive in China [E37], which is the channel that caps that export line.
- **Positioning**: managed money held 91,935 contracts in the week to 15 September 2026 [N48], the 97th percentile of its own record [N50] after peaking at the 100th in September 2026 [N51] and falling two weeks. That is what funds held, not a cause — but it is a crowded book, and crowded books make downside moves convex when the fundamental leg does not confirm.

My lean: the projected stock draw dominates the nearby read, because it is a high-confidence, already-published balance-sheet fact, while the warm-phase yield relief is medium confidence and still ahead of us inside its lag window. Both sides are real and the reader should hold both.

## The record

Newest layer by layer: the numbers are read through 25 September 2026, the newest dated document behind this answer is 22 April 2026, and the price tape runs through 24 September 2026.

- Carry-in for 2026/27 is 4.15 million bales [N9]; use stays at 1.5 million [N7][N8].

There is no figure for the seasonal pace against last year — not a level, not a change. The marketing-year export line is flat at 12.3 million bales [N5][N6]; that is a balance-sheet projection, not a pace read.

The supply-glut pattern and the supply-squeeze pattern are both partially lit on this market, which is the honest statement of a two-sided setup. On the loosening side, the Pacific warm-phase reading and Chinese carry-in stocks of 7.89 MMT [N123] both show; the Brazilian real at 5.18 per dollar [N126], the 44th percentile of its own record [N128], reads in the tail opposite the one that pattern wants and counts against it. Neither is in force; both are conditions to monitor.

## Mechanism
Stocks-to-grindings is cocoa's shock absorber. A low ratio means each tonne of lost pod output must be rationed by price rather than by drawdown, so the price response to a supply shock turns convex on the upside while a good crop is only slowly absorbed — an asymmetric, right-tailed setup. The driver model says dry Harmattan air and soil-moisture deficits in the Ivorian/Ghanaian belt tighten that balance at short lag (high confidence), while a well-watered belt raises the crop and pressures price.

## The record
- 2024/25 stocks-to-grindings: 28.52% [N1], from end stocks of 1,320 thousand tonnes [N2] against grindings of 4,628 thousand tonnes [N3], with production at 4,723 thousand tonnes [N4] — production above grindings, a rebuilding year.
- Standing: 10th percentile [N7], -1.66 sigma [N8], against a range spanning 0.26 [N5] to 0.48 [N6].
- History: 26.4% for 2023/24 after stocks fell 28% to 1.270 million tonnes [E1], reported 31 August 2025; 29.2% for 2024/25 in the ICCO release of 27 February 2026 [E7]; around 45% at the end of 1995/96 [E2].
- Weather now: West African maximum-temperature anomaly 1.53 z, August 2026 [N15], 91st percentile [N17]; longest dry-day run -0.92 z [N18], 3rd percentile [N20] — wetter than usual. The tropical Pacific anomaly is +1.8 degC, July 2026 [N9], 93rd percentile [N11], rising eight months.
- Tape: December 2026 delivery settled 5519 USD/metric ton on 23 September 2026 [N38], -410 over twenty-one sessions [N41] but +1209 over sixty-three [N42].
- Like state: the closest comparable tropical-Pacific reading is October 2025 — one case only. Over the one-to-three-quarter band the December 2026 delivery moved -2192 USD/metric ton by the window's open [N44] and -1049 by its close [N45]; one observation settles nothing.
- The chain from the Pacific anomaly into West African dryness: of eight past occasions this far out, the dry-day reading moved as the model expects in three and against in five; only one carries a price reading, too thin for a middle figure. The mechanism report behind that link is dated 20 May 2026 [E19].
- Data edges: numbers read through 25 September 2026, newest document 20 May 2026, price tape through 23 September 2026.

## Where the record disagrees
Two high-confidence West African readings point opposite ways. Heat at the 91st percentile [N17] supports the price-supportive West Africa deficit squeeze; the dry-spell reading in the 3rd percentile [N20] sits in the tail OPPOSITE the one that pattern names, so it counts against it. Two of that pattern's six conditions are counted here against three required — the squeeze is not in force. The price-pressuring patterns show none of their conditions. Net: I lean modestly price-supportive on the thin buffer plus heat, with the wet belt the live offset.

## What to watch

The fatter tail is on the export/policy side: the tropical Pacific sea-surface temperature anomaly reads +1.8 degC in July 2026 [N27], the 93rd percentile of its own record [N29], and the driver model carries warm-phase conditions as price-supportive for rice at one to three quarters, while India's exportable supply sits at an all-time-wide 25 MMT [N63] — an offsetting cap, not a confirmation. Both legs are live: a supply squeeze from Asian drought, against a record Indian export flow and record Indian carry-in.
raw_draft.postverify_mechanism:
## Mechanism
The physical chain here is short. US acreage sets supply; area is the lowest-quartile reading of its own record [N62], which drops production and pulls the stocks buffer down. A thinner buffer is what makes the response convex: with the stocks-to-use ratio at 27.31% [N16] versus 35.56% a year earlier [N17], the same size supply shock moves price more than it did last year, and deliverable US long-grain stocks at 1.28 MMT [N130] are the channel the model names for a thin contract detaching from cash.

The second chain is climatic and runs through Asia. The warm-phase Pacific reading is the largest move on this market [N27], at high confidence, and the model's mechanism is suppressed monsoon rainfall in India, Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines cutting production and triggering protective export curbs. That is a right-tail channel: it acts on world trade, not on US acres. Its declared window opens around February 2026 and closes around April 2027.

The price-supportive export-restriction pattern the model names is at or past its own count here — India's export flow, US ending stocks and the US stocks-to-use ratio are all showing, with buyer tender demand named but not read on this page. The declared amplifier is an export ban meeting panic tender buying.

The offsetting leg is real and same-market: India's carry-in stands at 58.5 MMT [N51], the 99th percentile of its own record [N53], rising four marketing years running, and Indian exports at 25 MMT [N63] are also at the 99th percentile [N65]. That is the world's swing supply sitting at its widest, and it caps how far a spike can run unless policy withdraws it. I lean price-supportive on the US sheet because the buffer is genuinely thinner year-over-year, but I would not call the world sheet tight.

## The record
- The tropical Pacific anomaly: +1.8 degC in July 2026 [N27], +2.4 sigma on its trailing ten-year window [N28], rising in each of the last eight months, read through the August 2026 data. A year-ago comparable state (February 2025) is the one case on the record readable on every dimension; the anomaly moved +0.18 degC by the time the lag opened [N154] and -0.39 degC by the time it closed [N155]. One case is history, not a forecast, and the November 2026 contract's record does not reach back that far.
- US 2026/27 projections, known 11 September 2026: production 158.2 million hundredweight [N1], exports 78 million hundredweight [N3], ending stocks 40.4 million hundredweight [N2], average farm price 14.9 $/cwt [N6] — the USDA's own projection for a year the record has not closed.
- The USDA season-average farm price fell from $15.10/cwt in MY2024/25 [N167] to $12.40/cwt in MY2025/26 [N168]; both are in-year USDA estimates at this as-of, survey-based, not futures settles.
- Managed money held 1,992 contracts net in the week to 15 September 2026 [N25], the 84th percentile of its own three-year record [N71], having risen in each of the last four weeks [N166]. That is what the reporting funds held, not a cause.
- Weather on the US crop is unremarkable: the drought reading was -0.13 z in August 2026 [N18] and heat stress 0.38 z [N19]; 73 pct of acreage was harvested in 2026 [N10].
- Dated documents: in April 2025 the attaché reported Indian government rice stocks ballooning beyond buffer norms, with higher offtake and open-market sales likely [E33]; the WASDE of 9 December 2025 raised 2025/26 global beginning stocks primarily on higher-than-expected Indian stocks reported by the Food Corporation of India [E37]. In April 2025 the attaché also reported that Indian export restrictions had reduced competition for Vietnamese exports [E38] — the restrictions themselves were loosened on 28 September 2024, when non-Basmati white rice moved from the prohibited to the free list subject to a $490/MT minimum export price [E39], about half a year before that observation. In March 2026 the attaché reported Red Sea and Middle East disruption raising freight and insurance costs for Thai rice [E43].
- How far each layer reaches: the numbers are read as of 26 September 2026, the newest known 25 September 2026 and the oldest August 2026; the newest dated document behind this answer is 31 March 2026; the board price tape runs through 24 September 2026.
- The record carries no figure for US rice crop condition ratings, nationally or for Arkansas, and none for total domestic use in 2026/27 — those are coverage gaps, not zeros.

## Where the record disagrees
The two loud readings on this market point opposite ways and both sit high in their own records. The warm-phase Pacific anomaly at the 93rd percentile [N29] is carried by the model as price-supportive for rice at high confidence, through Asian production loss and protective export curbs. But India's own exports at the 99th percentile [N65] and Indian carry-in at the 99th percentile [N53] are the physical evidence that the curb has not been reimposed and the surplus is there — the loosening that the December 2025 WASDE documented [E37]. The climate driver is a forecast channel with a lag; the Indian stock and flow rows are observed now. That is why I read the US sheet as tightening while the world sheet is not: the convexity lives in the US deliverable stock, not in world supply.

## The chain
Two chains reach through this board and neither settles a direction for rice today.

The first runs from the tropical Pacific anomaly through the Indian monsoon to Indian exports and on to a cotton market this question did not name. At the first link the anomaly sits at the 93rd percentile [N29], rising since November 2025, read through 5 September 2026; the model expects it to move monsoon weakness the same way, and the readings do not settle it. The monsoon link has no series served at all — the record is dark there, and the only dated document at that link describes an August 2017 weak monsoon that cut Indian kharif rice planting [E19], older than the lag the model allows. At the third link Indian exports sit at the 99th percentile [N65], rising since 2023, and the model's link onward carries no committed direction. The record holds no past case of Indian exports this far out with a downstream reading to measure.

The second chain runs on corn, from Chinese carry-in at the 84th percentile [N50], falling since 2024, into Chinese imports at the 89th percentile [N93], into US weekly export shipments — which peaked at the 97th percentile in April 2026 [N75] and now read the 85th [N74] — into the US corn stocks-to-use ratio at the 16th percentile [N99], falling since 2025. Each of those middle links agrees with the direction the model expects; the final link into rice carries no committed direction and the readings do not settle it. That series sat this far out twice before, and on neither occasion was a downstream reading published inside the model's lag. No dated document reaches the export-shipment link. Beyond these two, two hundred thirty-five chains of cause run into these three markets; the rest are counted, not followed.

## Spillovers
The same warm-phase Pacific reading is declared on three other markets here, each with its own sign: price-supportive for palm oil on the CME at a two-to-four-quarter lag, and at high confidence; price-pressuring for arabica coffee on ICE at one to three quarters, at medium confidence; price-pressuring for white maize on the JSE, where the cool-phase edge is stated at one to three quarters, at high confidence. Keep each market's own sign — one climate state, different signs, and it is one source of risk however many paths it takes. On CBOT corn and CBOT soybeans the warm phase is declared price-pressuring, the opposite of its sign on rice; across this estate the warm phase is declared price-pressuring on twenty-nine of the thirty-four other markets tracked and price-supportive on the rest.

## What to watch
- **The Pacific anomaly print**, +1.8 degC in July 2026 [N27], read through August 2026: it is past the line the desk calls strong and its run has not turned in eight months. It acts on rice over a window running 31 October 2026 to 30 April 2027. It reads wrong if the next print, due 1 October 2026, turns back inside 1.5 degC or the run of rising months breaks.
- **Indian exports**, 25 MMT for 2026/27 [N63], known 11 September 2026: this is the cap on any world squeeze, and it sits in the top decile of its own record. It acts over the zero-to-one-quarter window the model gives the Indian export lever. It reads wrong if the next print, 9 October 2026, returns Indian exports toward the middle of their own record — which is precisely the print that would arm the price-supportive export-restriction setup rather than cap it.
- **US ending stocks**, 1.28 MMT for 2026/27 [N130], known 11 September 2026 and falling over the last marketing year: this is the deliverable-stock channel the model names for a thin contract squeeze, and it acts inside zero to one quarter. It reads wrong if the next WASDE, 9 October 2026, revises US ending stocks back up.
Nothing else on this page cleared the bar for rice; the corn watch items nominated here belong to that market, not this one.

## Mechanism
The tariff channel is high-confidence and one-directional for this contract: Chinese duties on US-origin beans redirect Chinese demand to Brazil, the US export program slows, carryout builds, and the US benchmark is pressured while Brazilian premiums firm. It works through export pace, which is itself a high-confidence driver: a slow pace loosens the sheet, a fast pace draws stocks down. Against that sits the balance-sheet driver — a lower stocks-to-use ratio is price-supportive — and the crush, where a wide board crush pulls bean demand forward.

Where it turns convex: a thin stocks-to-use buffer means any further demand or yield shock has little cushion to absorb it, so the upside is the fat tail; conversely tariff-driven demand loss into an already-thin sheet is the loosening leg and is roughly linear until carryout rebuilds.

The warm Pacific phase now in force is declared to move this market in the price-pressuring direction at medium confidence, one to two quarters; its effect window, counted from the July 2026 reading, closes around January 2027. On palm oil the same phase is declared price-supportive at high confidence, two to four quarters — keep each market's own sign.

## Mechanism

**Direction.** Two loud readings lean the same way. The warm Pacific phase is declared to move CBOT soybeans in the opposite direction on a one-to-two quarter lag at medium confidence — above-normal austral-summer rain over Argentina and southern Brazil lifts South American yields and adds exportable supply to the sheet Chicago prices off. And the funds' position is a record-tail short: -126,674 contracts [N14], -3.4 sigma [N15], 0th percentile [N16], falling eight weeks running — declared same-direction, so on the model's own terms it amplifies rather than cushions. Against that, the crush is thin, not rich: the board crush margin was 0.81 USD/bu on 29 February 2024, the 11th percentile of its own record [N68][N70] — a reading that counts AGAINST the crush demand-pull story, not for it. I expect the supply-side leg to dominate inside three months, with the tight stocks-to-use reading [N146] the genuine offset.

**The chain this turn carries** runs from Thai soybean imports into the Chicago price. Thai imports were 3.24 MMT for 2021/22, the 96th percentile of their own record [N89][N91] but falling since 2020; the model expects that to move US export pace the same way; export pace carries no series here; it is expected to move the US stocks-to-use ratio the other way; that ratio reads 11.41 % of domestic use for 2020/21 [N146], 31st percentile [N148]; it is expected to move the calendar spread the other way, and the spread onto price the same way. No link's readings settle the direction, and no dated document reaches the first link inside its lag. Every chain carried here points lower for this market and none the other way. A second chain, from the same Pacific anomaly through excess rain and Brazilian production revisions, reaches DCE palm olein — a market this question did not name — and two of its links carry no series. Three hundred thirty-two chains of cause run into these markets; the rest are counted, not followed.
